analysis.one_liner: Shields raw-material suppliers to implant makers from most lawsuits over device harm.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 103rd Congress, the bill died in committee without ever receiving a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write federal rules for lawsuits over harm caused by medical implants. A patient could no longer sue the company that supplied the raw material or component part inside an implant unless they could prove, with expert affidavits, that the supplier delivered material that failed agreed specifications and that the defect caused the injury. The bill would override state tort law on this point, block discovery until a dismissal motion was decided, and make patients who lost a "frivolous" claim pay the supplier's attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that supply raw materials and bulk component parts for implants — specialty chemical, metals, and polymer firms. They would get near-immunity from implant-injury suits, a fast track to dismissal, freedom from discovery during dismissal motions, and fee awards against losing claimants. Device manufacturers would also gain a more secure supply chain, which the bill argues protects patients' access to implants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Raw-material and component suppliers to implant makers

how_it_helps.text: It would bar lawsuits against a biomaterials supplier unless the patient proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the supplier delivered materials that were not what was contracted for or failed agreed, published, or FDA-filed specifications, and that this caused the harm — a standard far narrower than ordinary product liability.

It would give suppliers layered procedural protection: the manufacturer must be named as a party, the patient must submit written determinations from qualified specialists before filing, no discovery is allowed against the supplier until the court rules on dismissal, and a supplier wins judgment without trial unless the patient's evidence could convince a reasonable jury.
It would require courts to make patients who name a supplier pay the supplier's attorney fees and costs whenever the claim against the supplier is found to be without merit and frivolous.

The bill's stated public-interest case is that suppliers of implant materials were exiting the market because litigation costs exceeded their tiny medical sales, and that without protection, suppliers here and abroad would stop selling, making life-saving implants unavailable and raising device costs.
It would supersede state law governing recovery for implant harm to the extent it sets a rule, replacing a patchwork of state tort standards with a single federal one.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by implants, who would lose the ability to pursue suppliers except in narrow off-spec-delivery cases, and would face expert-affidavit, fee-shifting, and discovery limits even in the cases left open. States would lose authority over their own tort law in this area. Device makers would remain fully liable, so the bill does not shift risk to them.

drawbacks.text: A patient hurt by an implant could no longer sue the supplier of the raw material or component part that caused the harm unless the material was off-specification — even if the supplier knew the material's properties and the harm was real.

The expert-affidavit requirements, the ban on discovery against the supplier until dismissal is decided, and mandatory fee-shifting for claims found frivolous would raise the cost and risk of suing, deterring some valid claims along with weak ones.
The bill applies retroactively: on enactment it would govern all implant-harm cases started afterward, including cases where the injury or the conduct causing it happened before the law passed.
It would preempt state tort law, taking the choice away from state courts and legislatures that had developed their own rules for supplier liability.

A good-faith objection to the bill's premise: the bill's own findings concede that courts have almost never held suppliers liable in these suits and generally find suppliers owe no duty to test or warn for finished implants, so the litigation burden the bill removes was already small — the main effect is to eliminate a rare path to recovery for patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine but narrow public benefit: if litigation costs were truly pushing suppliers out of the implant materials market, patients could lose access to devices. But the bill's own findings show courts already almost never held suppliers liable, so it would eliminate a rarely used path to recovery for injured patients while giving suppliers near-immunity, fast dismissals, and fee awards — a one-sided remedy for a problem that was, by the bill's own account, mostly about litigation expense rather than liability outcomes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 23, 1994, sent to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and the session ended in January 1995 with no hearing, markup, or vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Representative Ed Pastor introduced the bill on September 23, 1994, with six original cosponsors, less than three months before the 103rd Congress expired.
The same day it was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, a dual referral that splits jurisdiction over products liability and health matters.

In early October it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, and no further action was ever recorded.

The bill carried broad ideas that resurfaced later — liability limits for implant-material suppliers — but this version never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by implants kept the full range of existing tort remedies, including the rarely used but real ability to sue a raw-material supplier. Suppliers continued to face suit in theory, though courts almost never held them liable anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients kept their lawsuit rights

sides.party_line_note: The bill's seven Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and four Republican cosponsors crossed party lines, and no vote was ever taken that would have tested the split on the floor.

industries.industry: Biomaterials suppliers (specialty chemicals, metals, and polymers)
industries.note: The bill's direct beneficiary: suppliers would be shielded from implant-injury suits except for off-specification deliveries, get mandatory dismissal procedures with no discovery, and collect fees from losing claimants. Their gain comes directly out of patients' ability to recover in court.

Device makers would keep a reliable supply of raw materials and components, which the bill says protects patients' access to implants. They would stay fully liable for finished devices — the bill does not cut their exposure.

Suits against suppliers would shrink to a narrow off-spec standard, expert affidavits would be mandatory before filing, and attorneys could owe fees for claims found frivolous — cutting both case volume and revenue. Their interest tracks patients' access to the courts.
